# Skill: OpenCode

# OpenCode

Use this guide as the starting point for work involving OpenCode itself. It
covers the core concepts needed to configure and customize OpenCode, extend it
with plugins, and build integrations with the OpenCode SDK, clients, and API.

Full documentation is available at <https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/>. This overview is
only an index of core concepts. Before answering a question about a topic below,
fetch the URL named in that section and use the full page as the source of
truth. Follow links from that page when the question needs more detail. Fetch
<https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/> first when you need to discover the relevant
documentation page.

A machine-readable documentation index is available at
<https://opencode.ai/v2/llms.txt>.

## Version policy

Always answer for OpenCode V2 unless the user explicitly asks about V1,
legacy OpenCode, or migrating from V1.

Use only <https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/> documentation as the source of truth for V2.
Do not use <https://opencode.ai/docs/>, which documents V1, and do not use
general web search to resolve a V2 documentation question when the V2 docs or
linked pages cover it. The schema served from
<https://opencode.ai/config.json> accepts both V2 fields and deprecated V1
fields. Never recommend a field it marks deprecated. If V2 documentation is
missing or contradictory, state the uncertainty or ask for clarification instead of falling back to V1.

V1 documentation and syntax may be consulted only when the user explicitly
asks about V1 or when needed as migration input. Outputs and recommendations
must still use V2 unless the user specifically requests a V1 result.

## [CLI](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli)

For questions about the terminal interface, command-line invocation, `run`,
`mini`, terminal providers, or other CLI behavior, fetch the
[CLI guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli) and the relevant page linked from
that section.

CLI and TUI preferences are separate from OpenCode's server and project
configuration. They live in the global `~/.config/opencode/cli.json`, or
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode/cli.json` when `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` is set. There is no
project-local CLI configuration. Set `OPENCODE_CLI_CONFIG_CONTENT` to merge
inline JSON over the global settings. Most preferences can also be changed from
the TUI by pressing `Ctrl+P` and selecting **Open settings**.

### [Settings](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/config)

Fetch the full [CLI settings reference](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/config)
before editing `cli.json`. It documents every terminal-only setting, accepted
values, and examples, including themes, input, sessions, tabs, diffs, alerts,
Mini, keybindings, terminal plugins, and debugging. Do not put these settings
in `opencode.json(c)`.

### [Keybinds](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/keybinds)

Configure keybindings under `keybinds` in `cli.json`. The leader key is the
`keybinds.leader` entry; leader timing is configured separately under
`leader.timeout`. Bindings can use a string, an array of strings, or an object
when event behavior such as `preventDefault` is required. Disable a binding
with `"none"` or `false`.

Never guess a command ID, default binding, or accepted key syntax. Fetch the
full [keybind reference](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/keybinds), which lists
the current IDs and defaults, before answering or editing a binding.

## [OpenCode configuration](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/config)

OpenCode's server and project configuration uses JSON or JSONC. Include the
published schema so the user's editor can validate fields and provide
autocomplete:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
}
```

Global configuration lives at `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json(c)` and applies
to every project for that user. Project configuration can live in any directory
as `opencode.json(c)` or `.opencode/opencode.json(c)`, including nested packages
in a monorepo.

During ordinary project discovery, OpenCode searches the current Location
directory and every ancestor through the filesystem root, including directories
above the detected project or repository root. It merges direct
`opencode.json(c)` files from the farthest ancestor to the current directory,
then does the same for `.opencode/opencode.json(c)` files. This means every
discovered `.opencode` config overrides every discovered direct config. Global
filesystem configuration has lower precedence than these discovered documents.

Common configuration fields include `model`, `default_agent`, `permissions`,
`agents`, `commands`, `plugins`, `providers`, `mcp`, `skills`, `instructions`,
`references`, `formatter`, and `lsp`.

This configuration is distinct from `cli.json`. Use the
[CLI settings reference](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/cli/config) for terminal
preferences, especially themes and keybindings.

Do not guess field names or shapes. Fetch the V2 configuration guide and its
linked topic guide as the source of truth, and preserve unrelated settings when
editing an existing file. Keep the published `$schema` URL in configuration
examples, but do not fetch it to determine the V2 configuration shape.

See the [full configuration guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/config) for
every field, examples, config locations, and links to dedicated feature guides.

## [MCP servers](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/mcp-servers)

Configure MCP servers under `mcp.servers`. Prefer the CLI because it preserves
unrelated configuration. Use `--global` when the user asks to set up a service
for themselves without limiting it to the current project; omit it when they
explicitly want project-local configuration.

```sh
opencode mcp add <name> --global --url <remote-url>
opencode mcp list
```

Remote servers use OAuth by default. If `mcp list` reports that a server needs
authentication, tell the user to run `/mcps`, select the server, and sign in.
Do not run `opencode mcp auth` through the shell tool: it starts an interactive
flow whose authorization link can be hidden in background process output.
Use the user-facing MCP interface instead.

Report the server as configured but awaiting sign-in until its connection
status confirms it is connected.

OAuth credentials are stored outside the OpenCode configuration. Do not ask for or
store an API key when the server supports OAuth. Use header-based credentials
only when OAuth is unavailable or the user explicitly requires them, and use an
environment substitution such as `{env:MCP_API_KEY}` instead of writing a
secret into configuration.

## [V1 to V2 migration](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/migrate-v1)

For any request to migrate OpenCode configuration, agents, commands, skills,
plugins, integrations, or other behavior from V1 to V2, read the full
[migration guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/migrate-v1) before acting. In
the repository, its source is `services/www/src/docs/content/migrate-v1.mdx`.

V1 config files and `.opencode/` definitions are intended to remain compatible.
The only intentional breaking changes are the server API and plugin API. Native
V2 config uses more ergonomic shapes, but conversion is optional. When the user
requests conversion, inspect the complete configuration, preserve behavior and
unrelated settings, and apply only the relevant migrations from the guide. For
plugin migrations, fetch and follow both the migration guide and the full
[plugins guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins). If non-API V1
functionality fails in V2, use the `report` skill to file it as a compatibility
bug.

## [Plugins](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins)

For questions about creating, configuring, loading, publishing, or migrating
plugins, fetch the full [plugins guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins)
before answering. Refer to this guide when the user wants to build a plugin. It
covers hooks, transforms, tools, plugin context capabilities, and package
entrypoints. Plugins can also extend the TUI; for those, fetch the
[CLI plugin guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins/cli).
For custom methods and events shared with other plugins or clients, fetch the
[RPC guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/plugins/rpc).

## [Service](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/troubleshooting#check-the-background-service)

OpenCode uses a client-server architecture. Interfaces such as the TUI connect
to a background OpenCode service, which owns sessions, configuration, plugins,
permissions, and tool execution.

OpenCode normally discovers or starts the shared background service
automatically. If the service is stuck or unhealthy, restart it:

```sh
opencode service restart
```

Check its status after restarting:

```sh
opencode service status
```

## [API](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/api)

OpenCode exposes an HTTP API from its server. The API is described by an
OpenAPI document available from the running server at `/openapi.json`.

Use OpenCode's built-in `api` command for local requests. It uses the same
discovery and authentication flow as the TUI and may start the background
service when no compatible healthy service is available. It accepts either an
HTTP method and path or an OpenAPI operation ID.

Call an endpoint with an HTTP method and path:

```sh
opencode api get /api/info
```

Pass a request body with `--data` or `-d`, and additional headers with
`--header` or `-H`:

```sh
opencode api post /api/example --data '{"key":"value"}'
opencode api get /api/example --header 'X-Example:value'
```

Request bodies default to `Content-Type: application/json`. When OpenCode is
connected to an explicit server instead of its managed background service, use
the same configured server and authentication context rather than constructing
an unauthenticated request separately.

See the [full API reference](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/api) for available
endpoints, parameters, request bodies, and response schemas. The
raw [OpenAPI specification](https://opencode.ai/v2/openapi.json) is also
available for code generation and other tooling.

## [Client](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/client)

For questions about connecting an application to OpenCode over the network,
fetch the full [client guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/client) before
answering.

`@opencode/client` is the generated TypeScript client for the OpenCode HTTP
API. Its methods and types come from the same contract as the API reference.
The default entrypoint exposes Promise-based resource clients and async
iterables for streaming endpoints. The `@opencode/client/effect` entrypoint
exposes typed Effects, Streams, and decoded OpenCode schema values. Its
`Service` API can discover, start, stop, and authenticate with the local
background service from a Node application.

## [SDK](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/sdk)

For questions about embedding OpenCode directly in an application, fetch the
full [SDK guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/sdk) before answering. The SDK
hosts OpenCode in the application without opening an HTTP listener.

Use the [Effect SDK guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/sdk/effect) for
Effect applications. For Cloudflare Durable Objects, use the
[Cloudflare SDK guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/build/sdk/cloudflare).

## [Troubleshooting](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/troubleshooting)

OpenCode runs a client and a background server. Start by determining whether a
problem belongs to the client, the shared server, or one project.

- Check the service with `opencode service status` and verify the API with
  `opencode api get /api/info`.
- Compare with `opencode --standalone`, which runs the TUI with a private
  server, to isolate shared-service issues.
- Inspect `~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log`. Filter `role=cli` for
  client startup and `role=server` for sessions, providers, plugins,
  permissions, and tools.
- Run one reproduction with `OPENCODE_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` when normal logs are not
  sufficient.
- Do not delete or edit the database, service registration, or service config
  while diagnosing a problem. Back up persistent data before inspecting it
  with external tools.
- Redact API keys, authorization headers, prompts, file contents, and other
  sensitive data before sharing diagnostics.

See the [full troubleshooting guide](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/troubleshooting)
for service lifecycle commands, API inspection, log locations, explicit server
connections, issue-reporting details, and local development paths.

3: AstroAuthor is a blog-focused template built using [Astro](https://astro.build/) and [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/), forked from the [AstroWind](https://astrowind.vercel.app/) template. It is designed to provide a rich authoring experience out of the box.

6:

8: 
9: *   **Enhanced Markdown Authoring:** Intuitive Markdown syntax for common formatting needs.
10: *   **Dynamic Image Controls:** Control image dimensions and alignment directly from Markdown.
11: *   **Interactive Content Elements:** Collapsible sections and spoiler tags for engaging content.
12: *   **Rich Link Previews:** URLs automatically transformed into visually appealing link cards.
13: *   **Improved Content Navigation:** Table of Contents (TOC) for longer articles.
14:

18: 
19: *   **Sized and Aligned Inline Images:**
20:     *   Syntax: `![Alt text](URL#inline-30)`

23:     *   Syntax:

12: Dumbphone users have long relied on GroupMe for having group chats with kosher phone users.
13: When GroupMe recently announced that they're shutting down their SMS option, we were left scrambling to find an alternative.
14: 
15: As we work on bringing an alternative to kosher phone and dumbphone users, we have two models our system can use: centralized and decentralized.
16: 
17: A centralized system would rely on one provider, likely run by whoever builds this alternative.
18: 
19: A decentralized system would allow users to choose any service provider for chats, similar to how email works, leaving us to focus on building a kosher client.
20: 
21: While some might be inclined to go with a centralized option, there are multiple problems with such an approach that a decentralized system would avoid.
22: 
23: 
24: ### Covering costs
25: 
26: There are many expenses to running a group chat platform.
27: There are hosting fees, development and maintenance costs, and costs of cybersecurity.
28: 
29: If we rely on our own centralized platform, then all those costs fall on us.
30: Covering them wouldn't be fun.
31: 
32: A one-time fee isn't likely to be enough.
33: A subscription wouldn't work either.
34: Smartphone users won't pay, and it wouldn't go over well if only kosher phone users have to pay.
35: That leaves ads as the only viable way of covering expenses, which is problematic for a few reasons.
36: No one wants to buy a basic phone like a Kyocera or TCL, get it filtered to talk & text only, and then have ads appearing on their phone.
37: A basic phone is expected to stay just that, not act as a funnel for serving ads.
38: Same for the fancier kosher phones.
39: People don't want to be paying upwards of $300 for phones that will be showing them ads.
40: People don't want to be chatting with friends, or having discussions with coworkers, and have an ad for Moshele's Gefilte stuck in.
41: 
42: 
43: ### Monopolies are dangerous
44: 
45: Going with a centralized provider means that the provider will have a monopoly over group chats for kosher phones.
46: 
47: Whether you buy a Kyocera, TCL, Fig or Wonder, you are going to be forced to use that provider for group chats.
48: 
49: In the real world we see again and again that when a company has a market to itself with no real competition, it doesn't turn out well.
50: 
51: What usually happens is the company has no incentive to put too much work into maintaining the service well, they push more ads and higher subscriptions, necessary features are left out, and the users end up with a terrible product.
52: 
53: In this case, we won't be able to escape it.
54: As long as you have a kosher phone, you'll be stuck with this platform.
55: Getting everyone to adopt a platform isn't going to happen again.
56: 
57: ### Development and maintenance
58: 
59: Building and maintaining a messaging platform isn't simple.
60: 
61: There's the backend, which includes databases, security, and real-time message handling.
62: There are the apps that users will be using.
63: 
64: All that can be complex both to build and maintain.
65: If we rely on our own centralized platform, that will fall on us.
66: 
67: If we use an existing platform, we can offload those components.
68: 
69: 
70: 
71: ### Decentralized or just pre-existing?
72: 
73: You might point out that if we're talking about using an external provider, then why does it have to be decentralized?
74: 
75: The answer is that most centralized platforms don't allow third-party clients.
76: 
77: The ones that do only tolerate them, and there's no guarantee that they always will.
78: 
79: 
80: ![Typing on dumbphone](https://github.com/Dev-in-the-BM/In-Plaintext/blob/Main/src/assets/dumb-phone-01-68e3c18117b93.jpg?raw=true)
81: 
82: 
83: ### So now what
84: 
85: 
86: Out of all the existing platforms, two stand out as the best fit for our needs: Matrix and Delta Chat.
87: 
88: Matrix is a modern messaging platform, with a huge community around it, and likely as many users as Signal.
89: 
90: It has a lot of work and money going into maintaining it, and a large ecosystem of tools for hosting servers and building clients.
91: 
92: Delta Chat takes an entirely different approach.
93: 
94: It builds on top of email technologies, giving a chat UI and instant messaging features to good ol' email.
95: 
96: People use their existing email addresses, and can add anyone who uses email to chats.
97: 
98: 
99: ### Why should kosher phone companies care?
100: 
101: Why should Fig or Wonder care about how their phones messaging works?
102: 
103: The phones will sell either way, no?
104: 
105: Let's take a look at some recent news in the tech scene.
106: 
107: Apple released the MacBook Neo, their first "budget" laptop.
108: Rival laptop brands are desperate, trying to figure out how to compete.
109: 
110: What's the big deal?
111: 
112: Don't they already have better laptops for cheaper?
113: 
114: The problem is that their laptops all ship with Windows.
115: 
116: Windows, having a monopoly for decades, has rotted away, and is now slow, unreliable, confusing to use, and dated.
117: 
118: This makes even the premium laptops from Dell and Lenovo very unattractive.
119: 
120: All this, because they were dependent on another company that had a monopoly.
121: 
122: If kosher phone brands go with a centralized platform, and that platform can't live up to expectations, it can lower the appeal of the best kosher phones, making people look at them as cheap knockoff options.
123: 
124: Kosher phone makers, it's in your best interests to take matters into your own hands and make sure that whichever system kosher phone users adopt is one that can highlight your phones as premium devices, not draw attention to their flaws.
125: 
126: ---
127: 
128: When looking at the big picture, an existing decentralized platform is the only approach that truly makes sense, and I urge everyone involved in this to make sure that this is how we do things.

11: When I first heard about Keyphone, I was pretty impressed.
12: 
13: Between the hardware and features designed in-house, its modularity, and its minimal custom skin, it sounded very cool.
14: 
15: I kept listening out for updates, waiting to hear more details and news about it.
16: 
17: Eventually, Keyphone was available for preorder and I decided to go for it.
18: 
19: I got mine in the beginning of this year.
20: 
21: At first it was too raw to be a daily driver, and I ended up going with another phone for a while.
22: Within a half a year, they polished off the software and fixed up the keypad, and it quickly became one of my favorite phones.
23: 
24: Until then, every time I went back to the Keyphone, two things hit me right away: How it feels holding it, and its perfect UI design.
25: 
26: ### Perfect form factor
27: 
28: Most of the phones I've used as my daily drivers were big and clunky.
29: The Keyphone isn't just not clunky, it feels so *good* holding it.
30: Yeah, I know, they say it's "designed to live in your pocket, not in your hand", but you would've never guessed it.
31: It's a great size, feels solid, weight well balanced, sized just right.
32: 
33: ### Minimalist UI
34: 
35: The UI is another thing I feel they got right in a way no one else did.
36: Modern smartphones and apps are designed to be as appealing and immersive as possible, trying to suck you in every second of the day.
37: On the other extreme, there are dumbphones whose UI is functional but not necessarily very nice, and I personally prefer a more modern design.
38: Keyphone managed to achieve a beautiful balance, getting things right in the middle.
39: Modern, clean, and minimal.
40: 
41: ### Innovative features and design
42: 
43: In a market of dumbphones with UX mostly inspired by either Android or old school dumbphones, Keyphone brings a breath of fresh air.
44: Its launcher is unique, with a layout that's different, but easy to use, and optimized for a dumbphone.
45: They have their own custom notification and recent apps screens, which are simpler and a lot better suited to a small-screen button-phone, and a custom quick settings screen is supposed to be on the way as well.
46: 
47: The phone gets frequent OTA updates, bringing improvements, bug fixes, and new features.
48: This is another area I think they do a terrific job on.
49: I've seen other phones that prioritize shiny extras over bug fixes, and think that that's a big mistake.
50: Keyphone updates strike a good balance between bug fixes, adding missing functionality, and fancier features.
51: 
52: Upcoming features include their own maps app, email, and the ability to customize the functionality of the buttons on the side.
53: 
54: ### Dare to innovate
55: 
56: I've had a few conversations with the team at Keyphone, and one of the things I've seen is that they're not afraid to attempt what seems impossible, and are willing to think out of the box to be able to offer modern features while keeping things simple and undistracting.
57: 
58: Building navigation that can satisfy isn't easy, and most won't even try.
59: Keyphone isn't daunted, and their Maps is in the works.
60: When working on email, Keyphone churned out 5 solutions to offer email while keeping things simple, and then put out a poll asking users which they'd prefer.
61: 
62: I've sometimes given creative suggestions of what Keyphone can add to improve the phone, and they're always open to all ideas.
63: 
64: ---
65: 
66: ### Hard ware
67: 
68: Building a phone isn't cheap.
69: Designing it yourself is even more expensive.
70: Most small companies just have a Chinese manufacturer pull something from off the shelf and tweak it a little.
71: It's the cheapest and easiest way to do things.
72: 
73: Keyphone would only do things the right way.
74: 
75: They spent 4 years iterating and fine tuning.
76: 
77: When they saw that the original manufacturer they were working with wasn't able to make something that met their standards, Keyphone went elsewhere.
78: 
79: The first version of their keypads had some problems, but Keyphone kept going at it, and a few versions later, their keypad is very good.
80: 
81: All this paid off, and I think that the Keyphone is probably one of the highest quality modern basic phones out there.
82: 
83: It's very durable, and can handle a lot.
84: 
85: The buttons feel and click great.
86: 
87: It has an option for a physical QWERTY keyboard, and that was the feature I missed the most going back to my Wonder phone.
88: 
89: ---
90: 
91: ### What Keyphone *doesn't* have
92: 
93: The Keyphone is designed to be a simpler, locked down phone, which on the one hand means less distractions, but on the other hand means that it might not have features some want.
94: 
95: Things Keyphone doesn't have:
96: 
97: - Sideloading apps
98: - Flashing custom ROMs
99: - WhatsApp
100: - Music streaming
101: - On screen keyboard or swipe typing
102: 
103: These are all things that many dumbphones don't have, and are part of choosing to live with a basic phone.
104: 
105: ---
106: 
107: ### What I don't like about Keyphone
108: 
109: I usually go through this part with every phone I review.
110: No phone is perfect, and I want readers to know the limitations of phones they might buy.
111: 
112: When it comes to the keyphone, though, there isn't much for me to complain about.
113: 
114: Yes, there are features that are still being implemented, but that's expected with a new phone from a small company.
115: 
116: That said, there are still a few things that I think could be better.
117: 
118: The d-pad is very small, and at first was too small to be usable.
119: Like I said before, Keyphone's keyboard went through a few versions, and its d-pad is now a lot better.
120: It would be great if it was a little bigger, but it is definitely good enough. 
121: 
122: I've heard some say that the QWERTY keyboard is too cramped to be usable.
123: I personally think that while it is small, it isn't *too* small, and I find that typing works great on it.
124: 
125: I also think that making the soft-keys touch-sensitive was a mistake.
126: 
127: At the end of the day, all these might be a bit annoying, but aren't a big deal, and when contrasted with the other options, Keyphone is the clear winner.
128: 
129: ---
130: 
131: Overall, the Keyphone is a great phone, and keeps getting better with each update.
132: 
133: I'm very happy with it, it's the phone I use every day, and highly recommend it as a great option if you're looking for a quality, polished, basic phone.

14: ---
15: 
16: ## What is ADB?
17: 
18: ADB is a tool that you can use from your computer to do a lot things to Android phones that can't be done from the phone itself.
19: 
20: With ADB, you can:
21: 
22: - **Uninstall apps**
23: - **Install apps**
24: - **Manage app permissions**
25: - **Change phone settings**
26: 
27: Often, ADB will let you do more than the phone itself lets.
28: 
29: You can use it to uninstall apps that came with the phone, install apps on some dumbphones that restrict installing APKs directly on the phone, and change phone settings and app permissions that you can't set from the phone itself.
30: 
31: All this can be very useful for dumbing down devices, and extending the functionality of dumbphones.
32: 
33: ### Do I have to learn how to type up commands to use ADB?
34: 
35: While ADB is really a command line tool, there are a bunch of easy to use GUI apps that let you use a lot of ADB features without having to know any ADB commands.
36: 
37: See my article [over here](../adb-gui-tools) for some of the best ones.
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## The first time
42: 
43: Before you use ADB for the first time, you have to do some setup:
44: 
45: **Drivers:** If you're unfortunate enough to be using Windows, then you'll need to install drivers.
46: 
47: You can download a Universal ADB Drivers installer [from here](https://adb.clockworkmod.com/).
48: 
49: You'll also need to **enable USB debugging** on the phone.
50: 
51: On most phones you can do that by going to Settings > About phone > Build number, and clicking or tapping on Build number quickly 7 times.
52: 
53: Then go to Settings > System > Advanced > Developer options > USB debugging and enabling USB debugging.
54: 
55: On some phones you might need to repeat that last step every time the phone restarts.
56: 
57: The first time you connect the phone to a computer to use ADB, you'll get a popup on the phone asking you to authorize the connection with that computer.
58: 
59: On the TCL Flip 2, enable USB debugging by dialing `*#*#33284#*#*` (hint - 33284 is 'debug' on the phones keypad).
60: 
61: ---
62: 
63: ![Debloating](../../assets/changed_the_icons_202603292253.png)
64: 
65: ## ADB in the browser
66: 
67: If you want to skip having to install ADB apps and drivers, you can use ADB in your browser.
68: 
69: Just go to [app.tangoapp.dev](https://app.tangoapp.dev/) or [webadb.com](https://webadb.com/), and you have full ADB in the browser!
70: 
71: Browser based ADB works in Chromium based browsers including Chrome, Edge, Vivaldi and Brave.
72: 
73: It doesn't work in Firefox based browsers.
74: 
75: https://app.tangoapp.dev
76: 
77: https://webadb.com
78: 
79: ---
80: 
81: ## Scrcpy - screen mirroring
82: 
83: Scrcpy uses ADB to mirror your phones screen to your computer, and let's you control it from you computer.
84: 
85: You can [download it from here](https://guiscrcpy.srev.in/).
86: 
87: ---
88: 
89: ## ADB Commands
90: 
91: If you _do_ want to learn about using ADB the old fashioned way, here are some useful commands:
92: 
93: `adb devices` shows which devices are connected to the computer.
94: 
95: `adb reboot` restarts the phone.
96: 
97: `adb reboot safe` restarts the phone into safe mode. Can be helpful if you were tinkering and messed up.
98: 
99: Many commands start with `adb shell`.
100: 
101: PM is the package manager, which deals with apps.
102: 
103: `adb shell pm list packages` will list all installed apps.
104: 
105: `adb shell pm list packages -3` lists all third party apps you installed.
106: 
107: `adb shell pm install {path to APK on the phone}` will install an APK that's on your phone.
108: 
109: `adb shell pm uninstall {package name}` will uninstall an installed app.
110: 
111: `adb shell pm uninstall --user 0 {package name}` only uninstalls the app from the phones main user. This can be useful for uninstalling apps that can't be completely removed removed from the phone, like apps that came with the phone.
112: 
113: `adb shell pm disable-user {package name}` will disable an installed app.
114: 
115: `adb shell pm clear {package_name}` will clear the apps data, resetting it completely. This can help if you're having problems with an app that you didn't have before.
116: 
117: `adb shell am force-stop {package_name}` will kill the app.
118: 
119: `adb shell wm density {DPI}` changes the screen density. Lowering the DPI can make apps designed for larger screens fit better on a small dumbphone screen by making everything appear smaller. 
120: 
121: `adb shell wm density reset` resets the screen density to its default.
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## Shizuku
126: 
127: Shizuku is an Android app that allows apps to take advantage of ADBs superpowers, letting it do things that wouldn't otherwise be possible.
128: 
129: There are many apps that use Shizuku, including debloaters, app managers, and app installers.
130: 
131: See this [awesome list](https://github.com/timschneeb/awesome-shizuku) for a comprehensive collection of apps that use Shizuku.
132: 
133: https://shizuku.rikka.app/
134: 
135: https://github.com/RikkaApps/Shizuku
136: 
137: - - -
138: 
139: 
140: ADB is basically a master key for your Android. Whether you're stripping junk off a smartphone to make it dumb, forcing apps onto a flip phone, or just want to tweak your device, it gives you the control you need. 
141: 
142: With all the GUI tools and browser apps available today, there's no reason to be intimidated. Grab a cable, plug in your phone, and make your device work for you.

12:     Here's why you should avoid Google Play, and what to use instead.

16: 
17: 
18: ## The Play Store's darker side
19: 
20: While Google Play dominates app distribution on Android, and may appear convenient, it comes with several drawbacks.
21: 
22: It's dependent on Google Play Services, which is extremely invasive, resource intensive, and isn't available on all devices.
23: 
24: It imposes strict requirements on developers, making it not worthwhile for some hobbyist developers to publish their apps on Google Play.
25: 
26: Additionally, Google takes a steep 30% tax on all in-app purchases and subscriptions, reducing developer revenue and potentially making apps and services more expensive.
27: 
28: The following apps and sites are great alternatives to Google Play, offering better privacy, flexibility, and sometimes apps that aren't available on the Play Store.
29: 
30: ---
31: 
32: ## Google Play Clients
33: 
34: ### Aurora Store
35: 
36: Aurora Store is an open source, privacy-friendly app store that doesn't have its own library of apps. Instead, it downloads them directly from Google's servers, using reverse-engineered unofficial Google Play APIs.
37: 
38: It allows you to spoof your region and device model, allowing you to access apps that might not otherwise be available to you.
39: 
40: Aurora lets you install apps using Androids native installer, Shizuku, and root, and [this fork](https://github.com/alltechdev/dhizuku-app-installer) also offers an option to install with Dhizuku.
41: 
42: https://auroraoss.com/
43: 
44: https://github.com/whyorean/AuroraStore
45: 
46: https://apt.izzysoft.de/fdroid/index/apk/com.aurora.store
47: 
48: - - -
49: 
50: ### GPlay APK Downloader
51: 
52: GPlay APK Downloader is a website that, similar to Aurora, downloads apps from Google's servers. However, you don't need to install a separate app store to use its service.
53: Instead, you just download the APK to your phone, and can install the app directly, without any store.
54: 
55: It also offers an option to install apps directly from the site to your device, using web ADB.
56: 
57: GPlay APK Downloader is the best option for downloading apps from Google Play without having to use an app store.
58: 
59: https://apkdl.dietdroid.com/
60: 
61: - - -
62: 
63: ## FOSS app repositories
64: 
65: ### F-Droid
66: 
67: F-Droid is a repository exclusively for open-source apps.
68: 
69: Ironically, since most of these apps are built by hobbyist and end-users, instead of companies chasing profits, these apps are often higher quality than what you'll find on other app stores.
70: 
71: As all apps on F-Droid are open-source, it's considered the most secure source of apps, so the risk of malware is very low.
72: You can access F-Droid apps via their website, their official app store, or through third-party clients like [**Droidify**](https://github.com/Droid-ify/client) or [**Florid**](https://apt.izzysoft.de/packages/com.nahnah.florid).
73: 
74: https://f-droid.org/en/
75: 
76: https://github.com/f-droid
77: 
78: ### IzzyOnDroid
79: 
80: IzzyOnDroid is another repository of open-source apps, designed to integrate with standard F-Droid clients.
81: 
82: It has some differing philosophies than F-Droid, leading to it having a larger selection of apps than F-Droid.
83: 
84: It can be accessed in the same ways as F-Droid, through its website and F-Droid clients, and the Droidify F-Droid client comes with IzzyOnDroid enabled out of the box.
85: 
86: 
87: https://apt.izzysoft.de/fdroid
88: 
89: 
90: ![Destroying the Play Store](../../assets/breaking_google_play.png)
91: 
92: - - -
93: 
94: ## Sites that host apps themselves
95: 
96: APKMirror, Uptodown, and APKpure are the best sites to download proprietary apps from, that host apps the apps themselves.
97: 
98: The differences between these are security, curation, and the app store experience.
99: 
100: 
101: ### APKMirror
102: 
103: APKMirror is one of the most secure sites for downloading apps that are also available on Google Play.
104: 
105: They only host apps that are already available on Google Play, relying on the fact that Google vets apps before allowing them onto the Play Store.
106: 
107: They use signature verification to ensure that the APK they're giving you is authentic and wasn't tampered with.
108: 
109: Its downside is that it doesn't have an app store to install apps directly to your phone.
110: 
111: You have to first download the APK from their website, and then manually install it.
112: 
113: https://www.apkmirror.com/
114: 
115: ### Uptodown
116: 
117: Uptodown is another Google Play alternative with their own database of apps.
118: 
119: Unlike APKMirror, Uptodown also offers apps that aren't available on Google Play, which means that you can get apps that weren't vetted by Google, but they have their own security features to protect you from malware.
120: 
121: All apps are automatically scanned by VirusTotal, and the results are shown on the app's page, letting you choose if you want to trust the app.
122: 
123: Like APKMirror, Uptodown enforces signature verification, so if an app is also available on Google Play, then what Uptodown is giving you is guaranteed to be authentic.
124: 
125: Uptodown has its own app store, allowing you to search for, install, and update apps directly with their app, making things a lot simpler than APKMirror.
126: 
127: https://en.uptodown.com
128: 
129: ### APKPure
130: 
131: APKPure is the most popular website for downloading apps, but it isn't necessarily the best.
132: 
133: While currently its security is pretty much on par with APKMirror and Uptodown, it has had incidents in the past, staining its reputation, even though they've significantly upped their security since then.
134: 
135: APKPure allows you to choose which regional variant of an app to install.
136: 
137: Its bots scrape Google Play aggressively, often being the first one to offer updates to apps from when they're released.
138: 
139: It also is the only one to copy Google Play's ability to follow and get news on apps that weren't yet released.
140: 
141: They also keep the most archives of older versions of apps.
142: 
143: https://apkpure.com/
144: 
145: - - -
146: 
147: ## XAPK, APKM, APKS - What happened to the simple APK?
148: 
149: For over a decade, Android apps were built and installed as APK files.
150: 
151: Even if you got your apps from Google Play, the Play Store and Google Play's servers were dealing with APK files. If you obtained apps from other sources, it was as simple as downloading an APK file and installing it from Android's file manager. However, if you try to download APKs from websites now, you might notice that many apps aren't available as APKs anymore.
152: 
153: Instead, you'll be offered XAPKs, APKMs, APKS's, and other formats.
154: 
155: The reason for that is that Google has changed how apps are built and delivered, moving from monolithic APKs to split APKs.
156: 
157: Previously, the entire app, including all its code designed for various processor architectures, screen sizes, and languages, would be bundled into a single APK file. This often meant the app took up significant space on your phone for components that your device didn't need.
158: 
159: Now, with split APKs, device-specific components are generated as separate APKs, ensuring your phone only downloads the parts it needs.
160: 
161: While this is much more efficient, the standard APK file format cannot bundle multiple APKs. Google also didn't provide a new file format for bundling multiple APKs, leaving us without a native way to distribute split APKs outside of the Play Store.
162: 
163: A bunch of different vendors each tried solving this, leaving us with a bunch of new formats.
164: 
165: XAPK, created by APKPure, is the most popular, but APKS is also popular and widely supported.
166: 
167: Since Android doesn't natively support these formats, you'll need to use a dedicated installer app.
168: There are a bunch of great FOSS ones, including [InstallerX Revived](https://github.com/wxxsfxyzm/InstallerX-Revived), [Package Manager](https://smartpack.github.io/PackageManager/), [Package Installer](https://github.com/SanmerApps/PI), and [Split App Installer](https://github.com/aefyr/SAI).
169: 
170: https://github.com/wxxsfxyzm/InstallerX-Revived/blob/main/docs/README.md
171: 
172: https://smartpack.github.io/PackageManager/
173: 
174: https://github.com/SanmerApps/PI/blob/main/README.md
175: 
176: https://github.com/Aefyr/SAI/blob/master/README.md
177: 
178: - - -
179: 
180: ## Armv8, armv7, and x86 builds
181: 
182: Some developers, instead of distributing apps as split APK formats that aren't natively supported, choose to just build multiple APKs for each device type.
183: 
184: The most important thing to focus on is processor architecture.
185: You might see APKs for armv8, sometimes referred to as x64, and for armv7, and x86.
186: 
187: Most modern Android devices are armv8.
188: 
189: Older devices and Android dumbphones might be armv7.
190: 
191: x86 builds are for Chromebooks with AMD/Intel processors, and Android emulators on PCs.
192: 
193: ---
194: 
195: Whether you're daily-driving a dumbphone that doesn't support Play Services, keeping your smartphone degoogled for privacy, or you just prefer sideloading raw APKs without being tied to an app store, you have plenty of options. 
196: 
197: You don't need Google's official store to get the apps you need. With a little bit of know-how and the right tools, you can forget about the Play Store entirely and set up your device exactly the way you want it.
